elements.quote: Methods A systematic review of studies published between 2014 and 2024 was conducted across high-income and low- and middle-income countries.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states that a systematic review was conducted.

elements.quote: This study evaluated the impact of healthcare accreditation on quality outcomes across diverse hospital settings.

elements.quote: A systematic review of studies published between 2014 and 2024 was conducted across high-income and low- and middle-income countries. Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the date range and settings (countries) and number of included studies but does not provide clear, explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria.
The abstract does not identify the information sources (databases) used nor report when each source was last searched.
The abstract does not specify the methods used to assess risk of bias in the included studies.

elements.quote: Findings were synthesised narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guidance because included studies reported heterogeneous outcomes on incompatible scales that did not permit a methodologically defensible quantitative pooling.
elements.reason: The abstract states that results were synthesised narratively and cites the SWiM guidance, describing the synthesis method used.

elements.quote: Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies but does not report the total number of participants or provide a summary of relevant study characteristics.

elements.quote: Results Healthcare accreditation is associated with improvements in patient safety, organizational performance, and quality of care across diverse settings.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes (direction and domains of improvement) but does not provide numbers of included studies or participants for each outcome.

elements.quote: Findings were synthesised narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guidance because included studies reported heterogeneous outcomes on incompatible scales that did not permit a methodologically defensible quantitative pooling.
elements.reason: No meta-analysis was conducted (explicitly stated in the abstract), so reporting a pooled summary estimate and interval is not applicable.

elements.quote: The magnitude of impact varied across economic settings, with stronger effects in high-income countries compared to low- and middle-income countries, likely due to differences in resources and implementation capacity.
elements.reason: The abstract compares groups (economic settings) and indicates the direction of effect (stronger effects in high-income countries).

elements.quote: Conclusion The magnitude of impact varied across economic settings, with stronger effects in high-income countries compared to low- and middle-income countries, likely due to differences in resources and implementation capacity. The findings suggest that while accreditation contributes to quality improvement, its sustainability depends on contextual factors including governance, work-force capacity and system-level support.

The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide a registry name or registration number (the PROSPERO registration is reported elsewhere in the manuscript but not in the abstract).

elements.quote: Background Healthcare accreditation evaluates hospitals against established standards to promote continuous quality improvement. However, its long-term effectiveness on healthcare quality and patient satisfaction remains debatable, highlighting the need for enhanced standards and stakeholder support.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly describes the current state of knowledge (accreditation promotes quality improvement) and notes an important uncertainty (long-term effectiveness remains debatable), satisfying the requirement to describe current knowledge and uncertainties.

elements.quote: However, its long-term effectiveness on healthcare quality and patient satisfaction remains debatable, highlighting the need for enhanced standards and stakeholder support. This study evaluated the impact of healthcare accreditation on quality outcomes across diverse hospital settings.
elements.reason: The abstract states the need for enhanced standards and stakeholder support and frames the study as evaluating accreditation's impact, explaining the importance and rationale for conducting the review.
No text in the provided evidence explains the need for this review in relation to previous similar systematic reviews or cites/updates prior reviews.
Although the review assesses effects of accreditation, the provided evidence does not briefly describe any proposed mechanism of action of the intervention.
No logic model or depiction of hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes is provided in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: This study evaluated the impact of healthcare accreditation on quality outcomes across diverse hospital settings.

elements.quote: A comprehensive literature search was performed in the following databases: PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Medline, and Science Direct, from 2014 to 2024... Peer-reviewed journals should be in English and published between 2014 and 2024. Studies will be excluded if they meet the following criteria: ... Limited to editorials, commentaries, opinion pieces. Non-English articles and manuscripts without fulltext articles were excluded.

elements.quote: The narrative synthesis followed Synthesis Without Meta-Analyses (SWiM) reporting principles... summarising direction of effect, vote-counting based on direction, and key contextual moderators (income setting, accreditation body, hospital type). ... elements.reason: The methods explicitly define criteria used to decide which studies were eligible for quantitative pooling (convertible continuous measures, comparator data, dispersion statistics) and state that studies not meeting these criteria were excluded from pooling and included in the narrative synthesis, describing the processes for assigning studies to each type of synthesis.

elements.quote: Outcome commensurability for the meta-analysis was defined a priori as: (i) measurement of the same construct (healthcare-quality score derived from accreditationaligned domains - patient safety, organizational performance, and quality of care); (ii) reporting of effect on continuous scale convertible to standardized mean difference (SMD); and (iii) availability of pre-and post-accreditation comparator data, or accredited vs. non-accredited group comparison, with sample sizes and dispersion statistics. Studies that reported the construct only qualitatively, used non-convertible categorical outcomes, or lacked dispersion statistics were excluded from pooling and analysed narratively. The narrative synthesis followed Synthesis Without Meta-Analyses (SWiM) reporting principles... The following meta-analytic procedures were prespecified but not performed, as re-extraction revealed that included studies did not provide outcome data sufficiently homogeneous to permit defensible pooling (see results and limitations). For transparency, the pre-specified analysis plan is retained here. Cochran's Q test and I 2 statistics were used to assess heterogeneity; I 2 > 50% necessitated a random-effects model, while I 2 < 50% justified a fixed-effects model. The calculated effect sizes included standardized mean difference and odds ratio with their respective 95% CI. ... A random-effects model (Der Simonian-Laird estimator) was used because considerable between-study heterogeneity was anticipated... To assess robustness of the pooled estimate, leaveone-out sensitivity analyses were performed, removing each study in turn and re-estimating the pooled MD. Subgroup analyses by income setting (high-income vs. low-and middle-income) and accreditation body (JCI vs. national) were planned a priori. Publication bias was evaluated visually using a funnel plot and statistically using Egger's regression test, with a p value < 0.10 indicating significant small-study effect. All analyses were conducted in RevMan 5.4 (Cochrane, 2020).
elements.reason: The methods section explicitly describes how data would be prepared for synthesis: definitions for commensurability, requirement for continuous outcomes convertible to SMD, exclusion of studies lacking dispersion statistics, planned conversions (SMD), heterogeneity assessment rules, choice of meta-analytic model, sensitivity and subgroup analyses, and approach to narrative synthesis (SWiM). These constitute the required data-preparation methods.

elements.quote: The following meta-analytic procedures were prespecified but not performed, as re-extraction revealed that included studies did not provide outcome data sufficiently homogeneous to permit defensible pooling (see results and limitations). For transparency, the pre-specified analysis plan is retained here. Cochran's Q test and I 2 statistics were used to assess heterogeneity; I 2 > 50% necessitated a random-effects model, while I 2 < 50% justified a fixed-effects model. The calculated effect sizes included standardized mean difference and odds ratio with their respective 95% CI. A random-effects model (Der Simonian-Laird estimator) was used because considerable between-study heterogeneity was anticipated given variation in healthcare systems and accreditation frameworks. To assess robustness of the pooled estimate, leaveone-out sensitivity analyses were performed, removing each study in turn and re-estimating the pooled MD. Subgroup analyses by income setting (high-income vs. low-and middle-income) and accreditation body (JCI vs. national) were planned a priori.
